### C.2.3:8 - Common Anti-Patterns and How to Avoid Them

| Anti-pattern | What it looks like | Repair |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Status leakage | Approved content is assumed to have a precise interpretation. | Inspect the terms, conditions and inferences needed for the use. |
| Tool prestige | A prover or fashionable foundation is named in place of a demonstrated property. | Inspect the actual expression and the relevant checking evidence. |
| Appendix inflation | A formal annex is used to describe the whole argument as formally derived. | Assess the essential connecting inferences as well as the annex. |
| One ladder for different capabilities | Execution, hybrid modeling and higher-order proof receive successively higher ranks. | Separate their contributions and test the receiving requirement. |
| Profile as one Coordinate | Several characteristics are concealed inside one atomic F slot. | Declare the real slots or use an ordinary structured assessment. |
| Assessment replaces improvement | A larger scorecard is produced while a necessary predicate remains unstated. | Supply the missing expression and repeat its receiving use. |

### C.2.3:9 - Consequences

| Benefit | Trade-off and response |
| --- | --- |
| Adequate expressions remain usable across different formal traditions. | Comparison needs shared property meanings, not only matching numbers. |
| Formalization work targets the actual obstacle. | The recipient must state the operation and result that matter. |
| Composite arguments expose missing connections. | The assessment must include the relevant whole and its essential inferences. |
| Expression, scope and support remain distinct. | A concise assessment sometimes needs more than one sentence; it need not become a universal form. |

### C.2.3:10 - Rationale

Formality matters because an expression can make interpretations, operations and inferential commitments available for shared examination. The properties that enable these uses are related but not identical. A formal specification can define what is required without giving a procedure; a procedure can run without expressing a proof of the required property. A richer logic can express additional distinctions without improving an already sufficient statement of an ordinary invariant.

A profile preserves these relations without pretending that every pair has one overall order. Declared local chains remain economical when their criteria are genuinely nested. Comparison then rests on the receiving operation and preserved meaning. Composition follows the same reasoning: a whole must supply the connections its result depends on, while evidence about the world retains its separate role.

### C.2.3:11 - SoTA-Echoing

| Source and scope | Contribution used here | Limit of the transfer |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Kuhn (2014), [A Survey and Classification of Controlled Natural Languages](https://aclanthology.org/J14-1005/), §§3–3.2 and the qualification at the end of §3.4; established classification basis. | Precision, expressiveness, naturalness and simplicity answer different questions. Even the paper's ordered summaries are deliberate simplifications rather than an overall quality ranking. | PENS classifies languages. It does not directly rate an individual episteme, and its classes are not imported as F values. |
| ter Beek et al. (2024; volume edition 2025), [Formal Methods in Industry](https://doi.org/10.1145/3689374), §§1–2.2; contemporary account of industrial formal methods. | Formal specification, verification, execution and different verification techniques have distinct roles. Formal reasoning can apply to a non-executable specification; tool choice depends on the question and available support. | The discussion principally concerns computing systems. The profile and transdisciplinary receiving-use rule here are FPF's construction, not a scale claimed by that survey. |
| [Isabelle overview](https://isabelle.in.tum.de/overview.html), maintained tool documentation, including its HOL and LCF account. | A higher-order environment supplies formal statements and checked reasoning with substantial reusable libraries. | The availability of these capabilities does not establish that a particular submitted expression or proof has passed its required checks. |
| [The HoTT Book](https://homotopytypetheory.org/book/), authors' description of univalent foundations; foundational source. | Univalence and higher inductive types change what can be expressed and how mathematical reasoning is organized. | A different foundation is not a higher universal formality rank. Its relevance depends on the needed structures and admitted assumptions. |

These sources support distinctions among actual capabilities and formal bases. They do not establish a total order from prose through execution to successive schools of logic. Apply the assessment method above to the expression and use at hand; consult the sources when their particular language or apparatus is in question.

### C.2.3:12 - Relations

- **Uses:** A.18 and A.19 for declared Characteristics, Scales, profiles represented in spaces and any order overlay.
- **Coordinates with:** C.2 and C.2.2 for epistemic composition and assurance; B.3 when an assurance argument consumes the assessment.
- **Coordinates with:** C.2.LS, A.16 and C.2.4–C.2.7 for language-state properties that retain their own meanings.
- **Uses:** C.19.2 when selecting or configuring a formal apparatus is the missing practical contribution; C.39 when a way to obtain the result must be developed.
- **Coordinates with:** F.9 for a cross-context transfer whose mapping and limitations affect the receiving expression.

### C.2.3:13 - Distinctions for describing expression

The following descriptions identify common contributions. They are neither mutually exclusive classes nor consecutive levels. Select only distinctions needed by the receiving operation.

#### C.2.3:13.1 - Unstructured prose

Free natural language may leave vocabulary, assumptions and connections unstable. It can still preserve an observation or start an inquiry. Identify the ambiguity that obstructs the next use before requiring a more elaborate form.

#### C.2.3:13.2 - Scoped notes

A note can identify its topic and use terms consistently while leaving criteria informal. Naming the subject helps interpretation; it does not by itself formalize a predicate or narrow claim scope. Assess scope separately.

#### C.2.3:13.3 - Structured outline

A coherent section structure helps readers find claims and their grounds. Placeholder criteria can remain inside a complete outline. Editorial organization is useful, but inspect what the filled content actually defines.

#### C.2.3:13.4 - Controlled narrative

Constrained prose can stabilize interpretation and state acceptance or refusal conditions. This may be sufficient for a competent reader's decision. Automatic interpretation needs an additional mapping or semantics when the prose itself does not supply one.

#### C.2.3:13.5 - Explicit predicates and constraints

Typed entities, bound variables, units, domains and an interpretation make a predicate recoverable. The claim's consistency or consequence can then be examined under the declared semantics. A written formula with undefined symbols does not supply this contribution; an explicit predicate need not be executable or proved.

#### C.2.3:13.6 - Executable semantics

An expression can define how an interpreter or procedure produces results. Declare the relevant input meanings, operation and output interpretation. This enables a run under those conditions; it does not establish a separate invariant or substitute for its specification. A non-executable formal statement can remain sufficient for a mathematical argument.

#### C.2.3:13.7 - Coupled formalisms

A hybrid controller model can relate discrete transitions to continuous evolution; another account can connect several formal subsystems. State their shared meanings and interconnection obligations. Additional formalisms introduce relations to establish, not an automatic increase in rigor. Assess whether the whole preserves the properties its intended use needs.

#### C.2.3:13.8 - Formally expressed derivation

A derivation states how its conclusion follows from declared premises under an identified calculus. Inspect the essential inferential steps, including their connection to the stated conclusion. A checked derivation in higher-order logic can satisfy this need without translation into dependent type theory.

#### C.2.3:13.9 - Properties expressed in types and proof terms

A dependent type can express a property of a program or mathematical object; a term can carry a derivation of that property under the calculus. Recover the exact proposition, assumptions and term. Distinguish that expression from evidence that the required checker accepted it. Its usefulness may include preventing a particular invalid construction or connecting a program to its specification.

#### C.2.3:13.10 - Higher equalities and univalent foundations

When a question needs relationships among equalities or a particular treatment of equivalence, name those structures and the foundation used to express them. This can change the available construction or proof. It does not strengthen every unrelated invariant or make simpler formal foundations inadequate.

#### C.2.3:13.11 - Keeping the distinctions together

A useful assessment explains which of these contributions cooperate. A controlled requirement can be related to a formal invariant and an executable model, with a derivation connecting the model to the invariant. The links carry claims of their own. Check the required link when its meaning or assumptions change; do not infer the whole connection from the presence of all three documents.

### C.2.3:14 - Assessing formality in practice

#### C.2.3:14.1 - First-pass questions

1. Which claim, declaration or argument must be understood, executed, combined or checked?
2. Are its terms, domains and interpretation sufficient for that operation?
3. Are the required predicates, operations and inference steps actually expressed?
4. Which calculus and assumptions matter, and what checking result is available when required?
5. Would changing the expression property change the receiving result, or would it only add unused apparatus?

#### C.2.3:14.2 - Short assessment

A short assessment names the subject, required properties, observed basis and consequential gap. For example: “The interface condition gives typed inputs and outputs and an explicit postcondition. The procedure has executable semantics. The preservation of this postcondition across the retry branch is not expressed.” The next useful change is the missing retry argument, not the acquisition of a more elaborate specification language.

For repeated comparisons, use the same property meanings and conditions for every candidate. A compact profile can record them. Add a local rank only when its declared mapping preserves the distinctions used by the comparison.

#### C.2.3:14.3 - Typical improvements

- Replace unstable terms with explicit definitions and consistent references when interpretation is blocked.
- State a necessary acceptance condition as a predicate with its types, units and meaning when it must be evaluated or reasoned about.
- Supply operational semantics when the result must be computed.
- State the relations and obligations joining formal subsystems when the whole must be analysed.
- Express the missing derivation when the result depends on a conclusion from premises, then obtain the checking evidence required for that use.

These changes can occur independently or together. Describe the property changed; use a local rank difference only when the named scale gives it meaning.

### C.2.3:15 - Composition and interaction

#### C.2.3:15.1 - Essential-content and connection rule

Identify the assessed episteme's expressed claim or argument and its compositional support relation. A property of the whole requires the relevant properties of its essential content and of the inferences that connect it. A machine-checked annex does not make an informal connecting inference machine-checked. Listing common constituent properties is also insufficient when the composition can fail to preserve them.

External evidence has a different role. A typed claim supported by an informal observation can retain its explicit predicate and interpretation while its empirical warrant remains weak or unresolved under B.3. If the assessed subject is instead the whole argument, include its essential observation-to-conclusion inference in that assessment. Do not take a minimum over every external source in an evidence chain.

A minimum can abbreviate an upper bound on a local ordered scale only when all assessed parts use that scale and the composition rule establishes the bound, including the connection. A minimum alone does not prove that the whole meets that level; additional joining obligations may remain. Without that basis, inspect the needed properties directly.

#### C.2.3:15.2 - Relation to G

Formality concerns expression; G concerns applicability or claim scope. Making an assumption explicit can reveal that the claim applies less widely than expected. Record that scope correction separately from the improvement in expression. A precise claim can still have broad scope.

#### C.2.3:15.3 - Relation to R

An explicit expression can make a claim easier to test or its derivation easier to check. It does not create empirical support. A checked formal argument establishes its conclusion under the admitted premises and calculus; applying that conclusion to the world additionally needs the relevant interpretation and evidence. Assess freshness, corroboration and mapping limitations under their actual assurance models.

#### C.2.3:15.4 - Relation to CL and Bridges

A Bridge may expose loss or mismatch across contexts. Preserve that limitation for the receiving use. Reuse a formality assessment only if the properties and interpretation on which it relies survive the transfer. A receiving rewrite that changes claim content, EntityOfConcern or the effective reference scheme identifies a new episteme under C.2.1; assess the expression of that episteme. A changed carrier alone does not require a new assessment.

### C.2.3:16 - Worked examples

#### C.2.3:16.1 - Research hypothesis

A short note proposes a scaling law with stable terms and acceptance conditions in prose. That can be enough to decide which measurement to attempt. Writing the relation with explicit variables, units and parameter conditions enables a quantitative comparison. The expression becomes more determinate in those respects; the fit to observations remains a separate question. A poor fit is not repaired by making the same formula typographically more formal.

#### C.2.3:16.2 - Interface specification

An interface specification declares preconditions, postconditions and invariants with their types and interpretation. It can be used to compare designs before an implementation exists. A faithful executable reference model adds the ability to run scenarios. A running implementation that omits the postcondition does not dominate that specification: the two expressions supply different contributions. To claim conformance, connect the implementation behavior to the required postcondition and supply the needed argument or test.

#### C.2.3:16.3 - Safety controller

A controller and plant model express discrete transitions, continuous evolution and the obligations connecting them. A proof of an invariant in higher-order logic can satisfy a requirement for an explicitly derived invariant under those assumptions. A checked dependent-type development can satisfy the same requirement. Choose between adequate options by compatibility, available proofs and application cost through C.19.2; there is no general requirement to replace HOL with a supposedly higher foundation. If the plant-assumption evidence is weak, retain that limitation even when the derivation is fully checked.

#### C.2.3:16.4 - Decision policy

A policy says in controlled prose that a request exceeding a thirty-minute planned-duration ceiling fails the budget condition. To evaluate that condition automatically, introduce a Plan variable p, define plannedMinutes(p) in nonnegative real minutes and state `meetsBudget(p) iff plannedMinutes(p) <= 30`. The expression now gives the needed domain, unit and predicate. Its evaluation can answer the budget question; it supplies neither the other eligibility conditions nor permission to proceed.

If “duration” later means elapsed duration rather than planned duration, retaining the formula's printed shape is insufficient. The input interpretation and therefore the condition have changed. Return to the affected policy meaning and uses.

#### C.2.3:16.5 - Proof-bearing algorithm

An algorithm's dependent type states a length-preservation property, and its term expresses a derivation under the chosen type theory. Inspect the property and term, then recover the required checking result. A separate HOL proof of the same stated property may be equally sufficient for the recipient. If a new task instead requires reasoning about higher equalities or a specific univalent construction, it changes the apparatus requirement. That new requirement does not retrospectively make the earlier sufficient derivation less rigorous.

#### C.2.3:16.6 - Executable ML recipe

A training-and-evaluation recipe declares the inputs, parameters, operations and output interpretation needed to repeat a run. This supplies executable meaning. It does not express a proof of generalization merely because the harness is sophisticated. If the receiving use needs an empirical performance estimate, obtain the corresponding observations and inference. If it needs a formal property of the procedure, state and derive that property under a suitable model. The two continuations repair different gaps.

### C.2.3:17 - Guidance for developing and examining expressions

#### C.2.3:17.1 - For authors

Make the expression sufficient for its intended use. State a remaining ambiguity, unspecified operation or missing derivation when it changes what a reader can do. An early informal expression can be the appropriate result. Improve the property that blocks the next use, and preserve its connection to the original question.

#### C.2.3:17.2 - For reviewers

Read the assessed claim or argument and its actual expression. Check its terms, predicates, semantics and required inferences, including essential connections. Recover the basis for any claimed checking result. Keep missing expression, missing proof, weak empirical support and inadequate readability distinct, because they call for different repairs. A complete template or named tool answers none of those questions alone.

#### C.2.3:17.3 - For integrators and assurance leads

State the expression properties a receiving operation consumes. For a composition or transfer, establish their preservation through its actual connections. Reuse a declared local scale when it captures those needs; retain the underlying meaning when several participants use different scales. Apply separate scope, evidence, authority and language-state conditions where they matter.

### C.2.3:18 - Glossary and notation

- **Formality assessment (F).** An assessment of selected properties of an episteme's expression, with its subject, interpretation and basis recoverable.
- **Formality profile.** A structured account of those selected properties; when represented in a CharacteristicSpace, each actual Characteristic has its own declared slot.
- **Local ordered summary.** An explicit mapping from such assessments to a named ordinal scale whose levels have justified nested criteria.
- **Change in formality.** A change in an assessed property or in a justified order, not a numerical difference between unrelated labels.
- **Essential content and inference.** The content and connecting reasoning required by the assessed whole under its named composition relation; external warrant is assessed separately.
- **Example notation.** `F: explicit typed invariant; derivation not supplied`, or a threshold on a specifically declared local specification-expression scale.

### C.2.3:19 - Reusing an earlier assessment

#### C.2.3:19.1 - Recover the assessed meaning

An earlier label such as F4 or F8 is a locator for an assessment, not enough information to use it. Recover the actual expression, criteria and basis. Preserve useful properties already established, such as explicit predicates, executable semantics or a checked derivation. Do not infer a new profile or admissibility result from the number alone.

#### C.2.3:19.2 - Reuse a sufficient result

When the same expression properties and conditions still answer the receiving question, reuse the assessment. If an earlier requirement was written only as a rank, recover what operation and guarantee it was meant to protect before replacing it with explicit criteria or a justified local threshold. A binding requirement is changed through its governing authority; a revised vocabulary does not silently waive it. Reassess only the properties or dependent conclusions whose basis has changed.

#### C.2.3:19.3 - Boundary to language-state facets

This pattern does not redefine `U.ArticulationExplicitness`, `U.LanguageStateClosureDegree`, `U.LanguageStateAnchoringMode` or `U.LanguageStateRepresentationFactorBundle`. C.2.LS and its subordinate patterns govern those facets. A formality assessment can refer to their results when relevant, but must not relabel them as steps of one rigor scale.

### C.2.3:End

## C.2.LS - `U.LanguageStateFacetProfile` - Thin profile bundle for language-state facets

> **Type:** Definitional (D)
> **Status:** Stable
> **Normativity:** Normative unless marked informative

**Plain-name.** Language-state facet profile.

**Use this pattern when.** Use C.2.LS when the next use of a published `U.Episteme` needs an explicit profile of selected language-state readings and local thresholds. Select from formality, articulation, closure, anchoring and representation factors.

**Sufficient result and non-use.** The profile can point to existing readings and include only the facets needed together. If ordinary wording, one direct facet reading or an applicable existing profile already serves the receiving use, use it without constructing another bundle.

**What goes wrong if missed.** Teams replace the facet profile with a maturity adjective such as `ready`, `raw`, or `stable`, then use that label to choose routes, decide whether to reopen, interpret Bridges, or make publication decisions. The label hides the actual facet values.

**What this buys.** A thin, decomposable profile bundle: each facet keeps the definition and tests supplied by its own pattern, while the profile gives authors, assurance readers, and integrators one place to publish a threshold-relevant language-state position.

### C.2.LS:1 - Problem frame
To publish or compare position claims in the language-state chart over `U.CharacteristicSpace`, collect the needed facet references and readings in one profile. This makes the readings and their contribution to a receiving threshold inspectable while each facet pattern supplies its own definition.

### C.2.LS:2 - Problem
Without a dedicated profile bundle, authors blur articulation, closure, anchoring, and representation into one vague maturity story, or they silently reuse `F` as a surrogate. That blocks admissible threshold publication, undercuts `A.16` move guards, and makes school-to-school bridge work harder than it needs to be.

### C.2.LS:3 - Forces
| Force | Tension |
|---|---|
| **Thin profile bundle vs practical coordination** | Keep the bundle small, but still give one stable place where the language-state facets are named together. |
| **Reuse vs duplication** | Reuse A.18/A.19 characteristic machinery and A.16 moves; use E.18 only for an independently selected TransformationFlowStructure. |
| **Local thresholds vs cross-context comparability** | Contexts need local thresholds, but the facet names must stay stable enough for bridge work and viewpoint bundles. |

### C.2.LS:4 - Solution
`U.LanguageStateFacetProfile` is a typed profile bundle that names the facets needed to publish and interpret a position claim in the declared language-state chart over `U.CharacteristicSpace`. Select the applicable references from:

- `formalityRef` -> the expression-property assessment governed by `C.2.3`, including its selected basis and any justified local ordered summary
- `articulationExplicitnessRef` -> `U.ArticulationExplicitness` from `C.2.4`
- `languageStateClosureDegreeRef` -> `U.LanguageStateClosureDegree` from `C.2.5`
- `languageStateAnchoringModeRef` -> `U.LanguageStateAnchoringMode` from `C.2.6`
- `languageStateRepresentationFactorBundleRef` -> `U.LanguageStateRepresentationFactorBundle` from `C.2.7`
- `thresholdRefs?` -> context-local threshold declarations over the named facets
- `routeNotes?` -> informative notes that help interpret routing or reopening decisions

`C.2.LS` therefore defines only the **profile bundle**; it defines neither an individual characteristic nor a trajectory. A formality assessment or representation-factor bundle can contain several Characteristics. If placed in a CharacteristicSpace, each of those Characteristics receives its own declared Scale and slot; the reference to the assessment is not itself a Coordinate. `A.18/A.19` supply characteristic semantics, `A.16` defines admissible moves, and `E.18` governs an independently selected TransformationFlowStructure.

#### C.2.LS:4.0a - Kind and profile-bundle boundary

`U.LanguageStateFacetProfile` is a dependent durable profile-bundle value under the declared `U.LanguageStateSpace` and `U.CharacteristicSpace` boundary, not a root U-kind. Its identity is the explicit bundle of language-state facet refs used for position reading and threshold publication. A dashboard or table can publish the bundle; its display or label does not determine the facet readings or their admissible use.

#### C.2.LS:4.1 - Contribution boundary
`C.2.LS` defines only profile composition and requires the language-state facets to remain explicit and non-collapsed. It does **not**:

- redefine `F`;
- invent a universal formality progression or an undeclared local summary;
- redefine the scale semantics of `AE`, `CD`, `LanguageStateAnchoringMode`, or `U.LanguageStateRepresentationFactorBundle`;
- define reopen/backoff moves;
- define endpoint classification or bridge kinds.

#### C.2.LS:4.2 - Threshold publication discipline
Any threshold used to choose a next question, constrain an admissible move, or begin `A.6.P` recovery shall be published on explicit named facets in the profile. Do not describe hidden sub-levels of `F` when the real issue is articulation, closure, anchoring, or the representation-factor bundle.

#### C.2.LS:4.2.a - Local profile-reading witness
For this pattern, a published facet profile is reviewable when:

- the selected facet refs and readings are explicit or recoverable from a cited applicable upstream publication;
- any threshold-bearing use names the facet whose threshold is being invoked;
- route notes or local overlays remain informative and visibly docked to the explicit facet bundle;
- and any claimed move, Bridge, gate state or downstream result retains its own governing definition and test.

A polished label, one strong facet, or one memorable route note does not by itself yield an admissible profile reading. The profile remains conformant only when the named facets stay explicit and decomposable.

#### C.2.LS:4.3 - Composite readings
A language-state judgement may be composite, but the composite shall be decomposable. For example, a cue may be:

- low `AE`,
- medium `CD`,
- `AM.TraceAnchored`,
- and representation-wise mixed rather than purely symbolic.

A conforming profile makes this decomposition visible rather than hiding it under one stage label such as "early" or "raw".

#### C.2.LS:4.4 - Corridor map note
`C.2.LS` participates in the current `Language-State & Semantic Routing Corridor`, but contributes only the thin facet-profile bundle. Readers who need one map of the full language-state pattern set should read the corridor note in `C.2.2a`.

That map does not change this boundary: `C.2.LS` still does not define cue preservation, route-bearing publication, prompt entry, or downstream endpoint use.

### C.2.LS:5 - Archetypal Grounding
**Tell.** A team may say a draft is "still forming" for different reasons. `U.LanguageStateFacetProfile` forces the team to say whether the issue is low articulation, low candidate-space closure, an anchoring mismatch, or an unresolved representation-factor bundle.

**Show (System).** An operator alert note can have stable alert terms and structure, `AM.OperatorLoop` anchoring and low closure.

**Show (Episteme).** An inquiry note can be low articulation yet already tightly anchored to exemplars and traces.

### C.2.LS:6 - Bias-Annotation
Making selected facet readings explicit costs more than using one stage adjective. It lets the receiving reader test the actual threshold; retain the ordinary wording or existing reading when that already serves the use.

### C.2.LS:7 - Conformance Checklist
- `CC-C.2.LS-1` A language-state facet profile **SHALL** reference the patterns that define its facets rather than invent local unnamed factors.
- `CC-C.2.LS-2` `C.2.LS` **MUST NOT** redefine the C.2.3 assessment or conceal several expression properties in one undeclared rank.
- `CC-C.2.LS-3` Thresholds that matter for routing, reopening, or lexical repair **SHALL** be published on explicit facets.
- `CC-C.2.LS-4` Trajectory accounts that rely on facet profiles **SHOULD** reuse A.16 move kinds. Apply E.18 only to an independently selected TransformationFlowStructure; use E.18.2 when its mathematical description is needed.
- `CC-C.2.LS-5` Composite labels such as `early`, `settled`, or `ready` **SHALL NOT** stand in for the explicit facet bundle when those states matter operationally.
- `CC-C.2.LS-6` Composite readings, overlays, and route notes **SHALL** remain decomposable into named facets and **MUST NOT** behave as hidden master factors.
- `CC-C.2.LS-7` Profile references or notes **MUST NOT** replace the governing move, Bridge, gate or downstream rule. Cite the applicable rule when a proposed consequence depends on it.

### C.2.LS:8 - Common Anti-Patterns and How to Avoid Them
- **Shadow progression.** Treating `early/late` as a master scale. Split the judgement into the named facets.
- **Formality capture.** Letting `F` stand in for closure or articulation. Publish those facets explicitly.
- **Bundle inflation.** Turning `U.LanguageStateFacetProfile` into a second `A.19`. Keep it thin and referential.
- **Opaque readiness.** Using words such as `ready` or `mature` without naming which facet justifies the claim.
- **Route-note capture.** Letting an informative route note act as a move rule, gate state, or endpoint rule. Keep route notes informative. Use `A.16` for admissible moves, the applicable pattern for a downstream definition or test, the applicable gate or Work pattern for those claims, and an `authoritySourceRef` only when an external authority actually supplies the rule.

### C.2.LS:9 - Consequences
The benefit is clearer source and rule references: early cue work, bridge annotations, and reopen moves can all refer to one explicit facet profile. The trade-off is more explicit profile authoring and threshold publication.

### C.2.LS:10 - Rationale
The profile brings together the references needed to interpret facet readings and test a local threshold. Each referenced pattern supplies the corresponding definition and test; the profile preserves their different contributions to the receiving judgement.

### C.2.LS:11 - SoTA-Echoing

**Source boundary.** The facet meanings and profile rules come from `A.18/A.19` and the neighboring FPF patterns. The external comparisons below contribute scoped conditions and publication distinctions.

| Claim need | Bounded comparison | Exact source | Use in `C.2.LS` | Disposition |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Readiness claims should stay scoped instead of collapsing into one global adjective. | A profile can state scoped conditions and local thresholds rather than one blanket readiness label. | NIST AI RMF 1.0 (2023) | Require explicit facet-level thresholds and reject a polished profile label as a substitute for the facet values. | **Adopt/Adapt.** |
| A publication can keep several named description elements visible without making their container identical to those elements. | Architecture-description vocabulary distinguishes named elements and their correspondence in a published description. | ISO/IEC/IEEE 42010:2022 | Use this only as a narrow publication comparator; it does not establish the language-state facet ontology. | **Narrow comparator only.** |

**Local stance.** The useful bounded result is a small explicit facet profile with local thresholds and decomposable readings, not one maturity adjective or one route-coloured bundle label.

### C.2.LS:12 - Relations
- Builds on: `A.18`, `A.19`, `C.2.2a`, `C.2.3`.
- Coordinates with: `C.2.4`, `C.2.5`, `C.2.6`, `C.2.7`, `A.16.0`, `A.16`, `A.16.1`, `A.16.2`, `B.4.1`, `B.5.2.0`, `E.18`, `F.9` for any Bridge and bounded-use claim, and `F.9.1` only for an optional stance note about that claim.
- Constrains: language-state threshold publication and profile composition.
### C.2.LS:13 - Worked Examples and Composition Notes

#### C.2.LS:13.1 - Operator-facing early alert
A console alert note may be published with a language-state facet profile such as:

- its formality assessment states that the alert terms and structure are stable while some acceptance conditions remain informal;
- `AE = AE2` because candidate anchors are visible but the direct semantic branch or its required structure remains partial;
- `CD = CD1` because several routes remain live;
- `LanguageStateAnchoringMode = AM.OperatorLoop` because the note is directly anchored to operator intervention/work;
- `RepresentationFactorBundle = {local, sparse, mixed-symbolic}` because alert text and compact codes coexist.

This example shows why no one facet can replace the others. The note is not `simply early`; it is early in a specific, decomposable way.

#### C.2.LS:13.2 - Research cue before lexical repair
A felt or trace-anchored mismatch cue in an inquiry note may be:

- low `AE`,
- very low `CD`,
- `AM.EmbodiedFelt`,
- and representation-wise mixed because the cue is partly verbal, partly kinesthetic, partly exemplar-based.

Use the profile to identify what the next question still needs. `A.16.1` preserves the cue; `A.6.P` can recover an unclear relation, and `B.5.2` starts from an admissible `U.AbductivePrompt`. Apply the receiving pattern's conditions when choosing the move.

#### C.2.LS:13.3 - Architecture-description case
A viewpoint-bound note about the adequacy of an architecture description may state its constraints through explicit typed predicates, be moderately high in `AE`, still mid-level in `CD`, document-mediated in `AM`, and symbolic in its representation-factor bundle. The profile keeps description-side adequacy distinct from system-side engineering quality.

#### C.2.LS:13.4 - Same `F`, different profile
Two notes may supply the same required expression properties and still differ sharply in articulation, closure, anchoring, and representation factors. One may be operator-loop anchored and low-closure; another may be document-mediated and comparatively closed. The profile bundle keeps that difference visible instead of letting `F` behave like a master factor.

### C.2.LS:14 - Authoring and Review Guidance

#### C.2.LS:14.1 - For authors
When publishing a language-state facet profile:

1. start from the local authoring problem rather than from a memorized progression;
2. name the facet refs explicitly;
3. add threshold refs only when a threshold changes routing, repair, or another operative decision;
4. when a label such as "mature", "raw", or "ready" carries an operational claim, make the relevant facet readings and conditions visible.

#### C.2.LS:14.2 - For assurance readers
An assurance reader should ask:

- is any facet silently replaced by `F`?
- is a threshold published on an explicit facet rather than on a poetic surrogate?
- do route or reopen claims actually match the published facet bundle?
- do profile notes guide interpretation while preserving the definitions and tests supplied by the applicable patterns?

#### C.2.LS:14.3 - For integrators
Integrators should preserve the profile references. A local alias is acceptable when the underlying facet references remain recoverable and unambiguous.

### C.2.LS:15 - Extension and Migration Notes

#### C.2.LS:15.1 - Local extension rule
Contexts may extend the profile with local threshold refs, route notes, or additional descriptive aids, but they shall not add a new master facet that collapses the named facet set into one summary factor.

#### C.2.LS:15.2 - Migration from surrogate prose
When a stage label carries a claim used in routing, comparison or another decision, recover the readings it abbreviates. Examples include:

- "the episteme is still early",
- "the issue is not mature enough",
- "the note is ready",
- "the cue is still raw".

For that use, state the facet reading and its grounds, whether any relied-on threshold is met, and the governing rule for the resulting move. An ordinary description with no such operational claim needs no profile expansion.

#### C.2.LS:15.3 - Boundary reminder
Use the profile to refer to facet readings and applicable thresholds. Definitions and tests for moves, Bridges, Scales and bundles remain with their governing patterns.
### C.2.LS:16 - Profile Publication Package Discipline

#### C.2.LS:16.1 - Minimal publishable profile package
A publishable `U.LanguageStateFacetProfile` carries what its receiving use needs:

- the selected facet refs from :4, with their readings or references to those readings;
- any threshold refs that substantively affect routing, repair, bridge interpretation, or review load;
- the relation to `F` when readers might otherwise treat `F` as a surrogate;
- any missing or unknown reading that could change the receiving judgement.

One-line publication is admissible only if the facet definitions and tests remain legible.

#### C.2.LS:16.2 - Partial-profile rule
A partial profile identifies its selected facets and any missing reading that could change the receiving judgement. Publishing `AE` and `CD` can suffice when anchoring is irrelevant to that use. If the use depends on anchoring and its value is unavailable, state that unknown; a readiness label cannot fill it.

One facet can be sufficient for the named use. Refer to other readings only when that use needs them; no note about irrelevant omissions is required.

#### C.2.LS:16.3 - Overlay discipline
Local overlays such as "explicit-but-open", "trace-heavy", or "operator-tight" are admissible only when they dock to explicit facet refs. Overlays remain secondary to the declared profile and must not replace the facet bundle.

### C.2.LS:17 - Cross-Facet Reading Rule

#### C.2.LS:17.1 - No master-facet reading
Do not infer the whole language-state profile from one facet. High `AE` does not entail high `CD`; strong `AM.OperatorLoop` does not fix `AE` or `CD`; symbolic representation does not establish the expression properties needed by the receiving use; low `CD` does not imply low operational consequence.

#### C.2.LS:17.2 - Threshold interaction rule
When a threshold is expressed over one facet, say whether the other facets are merely informative or also constraining. An applicable local rule may allow entry into `B.5.2.0` once `AE` suffices for an explicit open question while still capping `CD` so rival answers remain live; it may allow entry into `A.6.P` at `AE3+` while still capping `CD` so the move remains exploratory rather than endpoint-binding.

#### C.2.LS:17.3 - Transition reading rule
Read profile transitions facetwise. A note may become more explicit without becoming more closed, more document-mediated without changing closure, or more symbolic without adding the expression properties needed by its receiving use. `A.16`, `A.16.1`, `A.16.2`, `B.4.1`, and `B.5.2.0` should therefore cite the facet transition that actually justifies the move.

### C.2.LS:18 - Review Matrix and Migration Tests

#### C.2.LS:18.1 - Review matrix
An assurance reader should ask:

- does each published facet keep the definition and test supplied by its own pattern rather than by surrogate prose;
- does any overlay smuggle a hidden scalar or gate decision;
- are threshold claims tied to the facet that really bears them;
- do cited moves in `A.16`, `A.16.1`, `A.16.2`, `B.4.1`, or `B.5.2.0` actually match the facet bundle;
- if reuse depends on distinct local meanings, was `F.9` used for the actual Bridge and its bounded-use claim, keeping any optional loss account or F.9.1 stance note separate from the facets;
- if viewpoint conformance is claimed, was it tested under `E.17.0`?

#### C.2.LS:18.2 - Migration test for source prose
When a receiving use depends on a source phrase such as "still immature" or "already stable enough", recover the claimed facet reading, its grounds, any threshold or route consequence, and the cited rule that warrants that consequence. Add an external `authoritySourceRef` only when an external authority actually supplies the rule.

#### C.2.LS:18.3 - Comparative profile use
Compare profiles on the named facets. A missing reading leaves that facet's comparison unresolved. A reporting aggregate needs a declared local model and operations admissible for the actual Scales under A.18/A.19; publishing an aggregation rule alone does not establish that basis. The aggregate remains secondary and must not replace the profile in norms, thresholds, or Bridge claims.

### C.2.LS:End

## C.2.4 - `U.ArticulationExplicitness` — How Explicit Is an Episteme's Meaning for Its Use?

> **Type:** Definitional (D)
> **Status:** Stable
> **Normativity:** Normative unless marked informative

**Plain-name.** Articulation explicitness.

**Use this pattern when.** Use C.2.4 when the next move depends on how explicitly a governed episteme's meaning is articulated for its semantic branch and receiving use.

**What goes wrong if missed.** A formal-looking sentence is treated as semantically ready, a real early cue is discarded as too vague, or a partly explicit note is forced through relation repair even when its receiving question concerns another kind of content, such as a plan or ordinary domain statement.

**What this buys.** One branch-neutral ordinal characteristic: a stable cue can acquire recoverable governed structure and a complete form for its actual semantic branch, with meaning that remains stable in a receiving use, without confusing articulation with formality, closure, truth, trust, or endpoint authority.

### C.2.4:1 - Problem frame
A governed `U.Episteme` may matter before its meaning is fully explicit. In the language-state chart over `U.CharacteristicSpace`, `AE` assesses how explicit that meaning is for its receiving use. The content may be a relation claim, a plan, a question or another domain statement; :17.1 gives the applicable branches.

### C.2.4:2 - Problem
When articulation explicitness stays implicit, authors either overstate readiness for a receiving pattern or hide useful early structure. Reusing `F` for this judgement creates a category error: formality assesses the expression properties needed by a use, while articulation concerns whether the meaning needed by the actual receiving use is explicit. A relation-shaped ladder creates a second error by scoring other well-formed claim kinds as immature merely because they are not relations.

### C.2.4:3 - Forces
| Force | Tension |
|---|---|
| **Early capture vs false precision** | Capture low-articulation cues without pretending they already have stable slots. |
| **Comparability vs local nuance** | Keep a shared ordinal discipline while allowing context-local threshold declarations. |
| **Branch readiness vs exploratory openness** | Say when a direct semantic branch can receive the episteme without forcing every cue through relation repair. |

### C.2.4:4 - Solution
`U.ArticulationExplicitness` is an ordinal characteristic of the degree to which a governed episteme's semantic structure is explicitly articulated for its branch and receiving use. It orders progression from a cue to a complete branch-appropriate expression whose meaning remains stable in a named receiving use. The common direction is independent of the semantic branch.

#### C.2.4:4.0a - Kind and characteristic boundary

`U.ArticulationExplicitness` names the Characteristic assessed here. The `AE0`–`AE5` readings belong to its declared ordinal Scale. A language-state chart binds that Characteristic and Scale in a basis slot under A.19; the Characteristic, a value on its Scale and the chart slot remain distinct. Local thresholds, route labels and table columns may reference them without introducing another U-kind.

#### C.2.4:4.1 - Characteristic specification
- **Kind:** CHR characteristic.
- **Scale discipline:** ordinal.
- **What rises:** semantic shape becomes more explicit.
- **What does not follow automatically:** truth, trust, closure, admissibility, or formality.

`AE` is therefore independent from `F`, from `LanguageStateClosureDegree`, and from endpoint authority.

Use `C.2.8` to compare how much selected structure a reader can correctly extract under stated preparation, access and budget, including when both expressions already meet the same `AE` threshold. Reader recovery supports an `AE` judgment about explicit articulation; it does not turn the `AE0`–`AE5` progression into a scale of extractable structural amount.

#### C.2.4:4.2 - Starter anchor set
| Anchor | Reading | Typical admissible publication state |
|---|---|---|
| `AE0` | a cue is felt or observed but cannot yet be stated as a stable question or contrast | preserve the source or cue without claiming a route |
| `AE1` | a stable cue, question, contrast, or disturbance is nameable | an early cue publication becomes useful |
| `AE2` | candidate anchors, participants, actions, fields, or meanings are visible, but the branch or structure remains partial | route candidates and missing pieces can be stated |
| `AE3` | the governed claim structure is recoverable enough to choose its direct semantic branch | the relevant repair or authoring pattern may receive it if the local threshold is met |
| `AE4` | a complete branch-appropriate form is publishable with the participants, conditions, and bounds needed by the current use | the direct subject pattern can check or use the publication |
| `AE5` | the meaning remains stable in one named receiving use, and a later change can be reviewed without reconstructing it from the source | the receiving use is straightforward; the level alone does not settle truth, closure, trust, or use authorization |

The anchors are a starter set. A local use may refine them, but it shall keep the common direction and the distinction from `F` intact. A refined anchor may be branch-relative; it may not make relation structure the universal measure of articulation.

#### C.2.4:4.3 - Use discipline
- An entry threshold may be stated in `AE` for the direct semantic branch named by the current use.
- `A.6.P` is only the relational branch. A note does not enter it merely because a table, arrow, or sentence looks relation-shaped.
- `AE` may justify why an episteme remains in `A.16.1` or `B.4.1` while its branch or required structure is still unresolved.
- A local threshold shall name both the intended receiving pattern and the branch-appropriate structure it requires.
- `AE` shall not stand in for closure, confidence, truth, trust, or authorization. Judge articulation and the C.2.3 expression properties by their own criteria; neither assessment label substitutes for the other.

#### C.2.4:4.4 - Change discipline
Raising `AE` requires additional recoverable anchors, participants, actions, conditions, bounds, or stable receiving-use structure appropriate to the current branch. Lowering `AE` is admissible under `A.16.2` when a prior articulation proves over-committed, misleading, or routed to the wrong branch.

### C.2.4:5 - Archetypal Grounding
**Tell.** “Something is off” may preserve a real cue while the meaning needed by the next question remains unclear. If the cue says only “role,” route it through `E.10.ROLE`; do not presume a work-facing kind or assignment.

**Show (System).** An operator alert cue grounded in a disturbance trace may be stabilized as a candidate intervention cue before the intended intervention and its conditions are fully stated.

**Show (Episteme).** A research note may name a contrast and exemplars before it has a fully articulated claim.

### C.2.4:6 - Bias-Annotation
The pattern legitimizes early cues. The counter-bias is explicit: low `AE` never licenses hidden semantics or unreviewable leaps.

### C.2.4:7 - Conformance Checklist
- `CC-C.2.4-1` `AE` **SHALL NOT** be treated as a synonym for `F`.
- `CC-C.2.4-2` A route change **SHOULD** require the local articulation threshold declared for that receiving branch; `A.6.P` applies only to a current relational branch.
- `CC-C.2.4-3` `AE` judgements that drive routing or use **SHALL** cite the anchors, participants, actions, conditions, bounds, or other branch-appropriate structure that justifies the chosen level.
- `CC-C.2.4-4` Raising `AE` **SHALL NOT** be described as if it automatically settled closure, truth, trust, authority, or admissibility.
- `CC-C.2.4-5` Relation-shaped notation **SHALL NOT** raise the level or select `A.6.P` when the actual claim belongs to another branch.

### C.2.4:8 - Common Anti-Patterns and How to Avoid Them
- **Precise syntax, unclear meaning.** A template constrains the sentence form while needed meanings remain unresolved. State the expression properties and the articulation gap separately.
- **Mystical cue immunity.** Low `AE` is presented as exempt from authoring discipline. Preserve it, but state what remains unresolved.
- **Ready-by-tone.** A sentence sounds precise, so authors assume `AE3+`. Publish the actual recoverable structure.
- **Relation-shaped shortcut.** Arrows, columns, or grammatical subjects and objects are treated as proof that the claim is relational. Recover the actual claim kind and route its branch before assigning the higher level.

### C.2.4:9 - Consequences
The benefit is admissible publication of early cues and branch-aware threshold setting. The trade-off is that authors must distinguish `not yet explicit` from `already formal` and must name the receiving branch rather than treating relation repair as the universal destination.

### C.2.4:10 - Rationale
`AE` supplies a shared ordinal interpretation for explicit articulation in the language-state chart. `A.16.0`, `A.16.1` and `B.4.1` can cite these anchors when an articulation threshold helps state their entry or completion condition. A directly stated sufficient condition needs no extra level merely to repeat it.

### C.2.4:11 - SoTA-Echoing
The distinction echoes work on sketching, focusing/TAE, embodied cue capture, and representation probing: a cue can be real and operationally relevant before it becomes fully explicit.

### C.2.4:12 - Relations
- Builds on: `A.18`, `C.2.2a`, `C.2.LS`.
- Coordinates with: `C.2.1`, `C.2.5`, `C.2.8`, `A.16.0`, `A.16`, `A.16.1`, `A.16.2`, `A.3.1`, `A.3.2`, `A.6.P`, `A.6.3.RT`, `A.13`, `A.15`, `A.15.1`, `C.29`, `F.6`, `B.4.1`, `B.5.2.0`, `C.2.P.DR`, and `C.16.P`.
- Constrains: articulation thresholds for routing and repair.
### C.2.4:13 - Worked Examples and Edge Cases

#### C.2.4:13.1 - Precise syntax, unclear meaning
A template may enforce precise syntax while leaving the meaning needed by the receiving use unclear. For example, a plan template can name a field without identifying the actual actor or the completion condition. A local system-role kind, classification, or assignment is selected only after evidence supports that branch. Formal-looking language does not make its semantic route recoverable.

#### C.2.4:13.2 - Plain plan, high articulation
The note `At 14:00, Maintenance Team 2 will isolate Pump P-17, replace Seal S-4, and restore service only after Leak Test LT-9 passes` uses ordinary language and little formal notation. It can still reach `AE4`: the planned actor, affected entity, ordered actions, time, and completion condition are explicit enough for the planning branch. It routes to `A.15`; the note describes planned actions, while `A.15.1` governs any admitted Work occurrence. The note needs no relation repair merely to count as explicit.

#### C.2.4:13.3 - Relation-looking but wrongly routed
A row `Maintenance Team 2 | Pump P-17 | isolate | 14:00` looks slot-shaped. If it records intended action, however, it is a compact plan row rather than proof of a durable relation. Its layout does not raise `AE` until the planning meaning and conditions are recoverable, and it does not select `A.6.P`.

#### C.2.4:13.4 - Threshold edge case
A cue with a stable trigger and candidate anchors may still sit between `AE2` and `AE3` because its direct branch is unresolved. Keep the cue recoverable in `B.4.1` or `A.16.1` and state what is missing. An applicable first recognition or clarification step can help select the branch; use its required inputs and apply the receiving branch's threshold before claiming that result. There is no universal relation threshold.

### C.2.4:14 - Authoring and Review Guidance

#### C.2.4:14.1 - Author prompt
To assign `AE`, ask:

- is a stable cue, question, or contrast nameable;
- which anchors, participants, actions, fields, or meanings are visible;
- is the direct semantic branch recoverable;
- is a complete form for that branch publishable;
- can the named receiving use interpret it without reconstructing the meaning from the source?

#### C.2.4:14.2 - Review prompt
A reviewer should reject an `AE` claim based only on rhetorical confidence or relation-shaped presentation. The claimed level should be supported by the branch-appropriate anchors, participants, actions, fields, meanings, conditions, bounds, or stable receiving-use structure.

#### C.2.4:14.3 - Threshold publication reminder
If `AE` determines whether an episteme stays in `A.16.1`, passes through `B.4.1`, or enters a direct receiving pattern, publish the local threshold and name that branch. Use `A.6.P` only for the relational branch; do not borrow its threshold for plans, methods, Work, representations, prompts, characteristics, or ordinary domain claims.

### C.2.4:15 - Extension and Migration Notes

#### C.2.4:15.1 - Local anchor refinement
Contexts may refine the starter anchor set with subanchors, but the refinement must preserve the ordinal direction and the distinction from `F` and `CD`.

#### C.2.4:15.2 - Migration from vague articulation prose
When routing or use depends on articulation, statements such as "still vague", "more explicit now", or "ready for formalization" should be migrated into explicit `AE` claims plus the corresponding move or routing claim.

#### C.2.4:15.3 - Boundary reminder
`AE` does not govern closure, confidence, or warrant. If authors want those meanings, they must publish them through their own governing patterns.
### C.2.4:16 - Articulation Publication Package Discipline

#### C.2.4:16.1 - Minimal articulation package
An `AE` claim that changes routing or use should be published with more than a level token. State:

- the exact episteme publication being judged;
- the stable cue, question, or contrast;
- the candidate anchors, participants, actions, fields, or meanings relevant to the current branch;
- the branch-appropriate structure already recoverable and any decision-relevant gap;
- the grounds for the level;
- the named next use and its local threshold when the level is used to change route.

Unresolved claim-bearing `role` wording goes first to `E.10.ROLE`. A bare `AE3` label is insufficient when the supporting structure and intended receiving branch are absent.

#### C.2.4:16.2 - Threshold package for route change
When `AE` controls a route change, publish the intended receiving pattern, its semantic branch, the minimum recoverable structure it requires, and the current evidence that the publication meets or misses that threshold. A relational route may name `A.6.P`; another branch names its own receiving pattern.

#### C.2.4:16.3 - Evidence-limited rise rule
`AE` may rise only as far as the published branch-appropriate structure—including any relevant anchors, slots, or contrasts—warrants. Stylistic polish, templates, or rhetorical confidence do not raise `AE` on their own.

### C.2.4:17 - Threshold Crossing and Split Handling

#### C.2.4:17.1 - Branch-aware high-articulation exits
At `AE3+`, use the local threshold of the direct branch rather than one universal destination:

- for an actual relation claim, restore precision through `A.6.P` when needed, then use its direct relation pattern;
- for a plan or intended activity, use `A.15`;
- for a Method, use `A.3.1`; use `A.3.2` to test a `C.2.1` episteme's membership as a MethodDescription;
- for a dated Work-occurrence claim, recover the performer under `A.13` and independently test Work admission under `A.15.1`; use `F.6` only when precise assignment-bound attribution is needed;
- for a representation claim, use `C.29` and the represented subject's rule; use `C.2.P.DR` when declarative form is being overread, adding `A.6.3.RT` only when a representation transition is current;
- for an abductive prompt or explicit open question, use `B.5.2.0` or the direct question pattern;
- for a Characteristic or Scale claim, use `A.17` and `A.18`, with `C.16.P` when its scalar wording hides the construction;
- for an ordinary domain claim, use the domain pattern that governs its subject; use `C.2.1` when episteme identity is needed.

If the branch or threshold is unresolved, preserve the episteme through `B.4.1` or `A.16.1` and state what is missing. Use an applicable recognition or clarification step to resolve that question before relying on the receiving result. `AE` reports recoverable articulation; it does not itself choose the branch or authorize the receiving use.

#### C.2.4:17.2 - High-articulation, low-closure cases
A note may reach `AE4+` while remaining low or mid in `CD`. In such cases state that articulation is sufficient for precise handling while closure still leaves rival routes or frames live.

#### C.2.4:17.3 - Articulation claims for separate fragments
Scope each fragment's articulation claim to its receiving use; do not assign one averaged level that hides the actual route structure. The fragments may remain in the same note or publication when their scopes are clear.

### C.2.4:18 - Review Matrix and Endpoint Boundary Tests

#### C.2.4:18.1 - Review matrix
A reviewer should ask:

- are the named anchors present in the published expression rather than presupposed;
- does the level rest on recoverable meaning rather than tone, formatting, arrows, or columns;
- is the direct semantic branch explicit, or is a relation route being inferred from presentation alone;
- are the participants, actions, fields, meanings, conditions, bounds, or ordinary wording required by that branch still hidden;
- has an intended activity or plan been mislabeled as Tech `Work` before an occurrence is admitted;
- if `AE` justifies a route change, does the publication meet the named receiving pattern's entry conditions?

#### C.2.4:18.2 - Endpoint-boundary test
High `AE` does not by itself authorize endpoint claims, gate claims, or quality ascriptions. If such consequences appear, show which downstream governing pattern takes over.

#### C.2.4:18.3 - Migration note for false precision
Rigid templates, capitalized labels, or tidy sentence rhythm can simulate articulation. Test whether the claimed branch-appropriate structure, including any required anchors or slots, is recoverable. If it is not, revise the assessment to the level supported by the available structure, or leave the level unresolved when its grounds cannot be established.

### C.2.4:End

## C.2.5 - `U.LanguageStateClosureDegree` — How Fixed Is the Current Candidate Space?

> **Type:** Definitional (D)
> **Status:** Stable
> **Normativity:** Normative unless marked informative

**Plain-name.** Language-state closure degree.

**Use this pattern when.** Use C.2.5 when a governed `U.Episteme` publication must say how fixed its candidate space, route space, or frame space has become before endpoint use, reopening, or retreat.

**What goes wrong if missed.** A confident tone is mistaken for closure, closure is mistaken for truth or gate authority, or a closure drop leaves readers unable to tell which endpoint uses and route commitments remain supported.

**What this buys.** A separate ordinal characteristic for closure degree, so teams can distinguish exploration, stabilization, selected route, guarded fixation, and admissible retreat without collapsing closure into formality, articulation, warrant, or obligation.

### C.2.5:1 - Problem frame
A governed `U.Episteme` may already be explicit enough for publication while its declared position claim remains intentionally open to rival routes or frames. The declared language-state chart over `U.CharacteristicSpace` therefore needs a separate pattern defining the closure-degree basis slot: how fixed or closed the current candidate space has become.

### C.2.5:2 - Problem
Closure is often hidden inside vague words such as "ready", "settled", or "open". When closure is not explicit, teams cannot reason cleanly about reopen, sketch-backoff, or the admissibility of endpoint docking.

### C.2.5:3 - Forces
| Force | Tension |
|---|---|
| **Commitment vs exploration** | Preserve open search without losing auditability. |
| **Stability vs reversibility** | Allow closure increases, but also admissible reopening and reframing. |
| **Authority vs explicit retreat** | Let strong closure matter, but keep visible the moves that relax it. |

### C.2.5:4 - Solution
`U.LanguageStateClosureDegree` is an ordinal characteristic over how fixed the current candidate set, framing, and admissible next moves are in a published position claim in the declared language-state chart over `U.CharacteristicSpace`.

#### C.2.5:4.0a - Kind and characteristic boundary

`U.LanguageStateClosureDegree` names the Characteristic assessed here. The `CD0`–`CD5` readings belong to its ordinal Scale. A language-state chart binds that Characteristic and Scale in a basis slot under A.19; the Characteristic, a value on its Scale and the chart slot remain distinct. Claims about local route commitments, gates, or authority states remain separate from the closure-degree claim. When one matters to the current use, test it against its applicable rule and current case facts.

#### C.2.5:4.1 - Characteristic specification
- **Kind:** CHR characteristic.
- **Scale discipline:** ordinal.
- **What rises:** the candidate space or selected route becomes more fixed for the named use. Any binding force comes from its separately established rule.
- **What does not follow automatically:** truth, trust, formality, or quality.

#### C.2.5:4.2 - Starter anchor set
| Anchor | Reading | Typical interpretation for use |
|---|---|---|
| `CD0` | exploratory-open | broad rival space remains live |
| `CD1` | weakly stabilized | some contrasts are present, but rival routes remain normal |
| `CD2` | narrowed candidate space | explicit rivals remain, but the field is meaningfully reduced |
| `CD3` | selected route or framing | one route is chosen, though reopening remains routine |
| `CD4` | publication- or operation-fixed under guard | changes require named justification |
| `CD5` | strongly fixed | relaxation requires an explicit `A.16.2` move and governance note |

#### C.2.5:4.3 - Non-collapse rules
`LanguageStateClosureDegree` is not:

- `F`;
- articulation explicitness;
- gate decision;
- evaluator confidence;
- warrant strength.

A text may be highly explicit but low-closure, or low-explicitness but already high-closure by policy. Those states shall not be collapsed.

#### C.2.5:4.4 - Change discipline
Increasing `CD` requires narrowing candidate space, route space, or frame space explicitly. Lowering `CD` is admissible only through a named move such as `reopen`, `sketchBackoff`, or `respecify`, with a retained-witness and discarded-assumption note.

An ordinary PatternID in `governingPatternRef` locates the FPF rule relevant to the closure claim. Use a separate `relationFunctionClaimRef` for its exact defining or constraining `ClaimGraph` only when admissible interpretation, comparison, migration, publication, or reuse depends on that exact rule identity (`E.10`, `E.4.PFR`). Use `authoritySourceRef` when a non-pattern source carries the relevant authority.

### C.2.5:5 - Archetypal Grounding
**Tell.** Two notes may look equally explicit, but one is still intentionally open while the other is already committed to a single route.

**Show (System).** An incident cue can be routed to rollback while remaining reopenable if new evidence arrives.

**Show (Episteme).** A hypothesis sketch can be highly articulated but still low closure because rival explanations remain live.

### C.2.5:6 - Bias-Annotation
Explicit closure takes description work; it makes the remaining rivals and grounds of fixation recoverable.

### C.2.5:7 - Conformance Checklist
- `CC-C.2.5-1` Closure **SHALL** be declared independently from `F` and `AE` when it matters for routing, docking, or reopening.
- `CC-C.2.5-2` Reopen/backoff moves **SHALL** cite the prior closure state they are relaxing.
- `CC-C.2.5-3` Strong-closure states **SHOULD** name the guard, `governingPatternRef`, or `authoritySourceRef` that makes the closure binding.
- `CC-C.2.5-4` A closure drop **SHALL NOT** silently preserve an endpoint-use claim when the supporting route or publication form no longer supports it.

### C.2.5:8 - Common Anti-Patterns and How to Avoid Them
- **Closure by mood.** A sentence sounds decisive, so teams assume high closure. State the actual fixation and its grounds; add a `CD` reading when the receiving use needs that scale.
- **Irreversible drift.** Closure rises informally but no reopening condition exists. Use `A.16.2`.
- **Authority smuggling.** High closure is treated as if it were automatically a gate or obligation. Check the applicable gate condition for a gate claim; use `A.2.8` to check whether the claimed obligation obtains.

### C.2.5:9 - Consequences
The benefit is admissible handling of stabilization, commitment, and reopening. The trade-off is more explicit state declaration and more explicit retreat records.

### C.2.5:10 - Rationale
Closure describes how fixed the candidate space is; articulation describes how explicit its meaning is. `A.16.0` and its related patterns can use both when each affects the move condition.

### C.2.5:11 - SoTA-Echoing
The facet aligns with iterative design, open-world reasoning, and exploratory search practices where closure is a governance choice rather than a hidden by-product.

### C.2.5:12 - Relations
- Builds on: `A.18`, `C.2.2a`, `C.2.LS`.
- Coordinates with: `C.2.4`, `A.16.0`, `A.16`, `A.16.1`, `A.16.2`, `B.4.1`, `B.5.2.0`.
- Constrains: reopen, backoff, and endpoint docking guards.
### C.2.5:13 - Worked Examples and Retreat Cases

#### C.2.5:13.1 - Explicit but still open
A note may sit at `AE4` yet only `CD1` because rival explanatory frames are still live. Explicit publication does not imply settled closure.

#### C.2.5:13.2 - Strong closure under policy guard
An operator rule may be only moderate in `AE` but high in `CD` because policy already fixes the next step under the current horizon. This shows why closure is governance-facing, not merely stylistic.

#### C.2.5:13.3 - Reopen case
A route may move from `CD4` back to `CD2` when counter-evidence appears. Record the counter-evidence and the retreat as an admissible `A.16.2` move.

### C.2.5:14 - Authoring and Review Guidance

#### C.2.5:14.1 - Author prompt
To assign `CD`, ask:

- how many rivals remain live?
- is one route merely preferred, or actually fixed?
- if the closure is binding, what applicable guard, `governingPatternRef`, or `authoritySourceRef` makes it so?
- what would count as an admissible reopen trigger?

#### C.2.5:14.2 - Review prompt
An assurance reader should identify the actual narrowing and its source under :16.2, including a policy or protocol when it fixes the route. Confident tone or an appeal to hierarchy alone does not establish that fixity.

#### C.2.5:14.3 - Governance note
Whenever a claim about a gate, commitment, or endpoint use depends on `CD`, the supporting guard, `governingPatternRef`, or `authoritySourceRef` should be visible.

### C.2.5:15 - Extension and Migration Notes

#### C.2.5:15.1 - Local anchor refinement
Contexts may refine the starter closure anchors, but shall keep the ordinal progression and the explicit link to reopen/backoff discipline.

#### C.2.5:15.2 - Migration from readiness language
When routing, endpoint use or reopening depends on words such as "settled", "closed", "final", or "open", recover the claimed fixity and its grounds. Use an explicit `CD` reading when that scale is needed and a named `A.16.2` move when the closure changes. Sufficient ordinary wording needs no separate level solely to repeat it.

#### C.2.5:15.3 - Boundary reminder
`CD` is not warrant strength and not a gate decision. It speaks only about the local fixity of the current episteme or publication position and its candidate space.
### C.2.5:16 - Closure Publication Package Discipline

#### C.2.5:16.1 - Minimal closure package
A publishable `CD` claim should name what has narrowed:

- the rival routes or frames that remain live;
- the route, frame, or interpretation that is currently privileged or fixed;
- any guard, `governingPatternRef`, `authoritySourceRef`, or policy that makes the narrowing binding;
- the condition under which an admissible reopen or backoff would occur.

A bare claim such as "now settled" is insufficient when closure affects routing or authority.

#### C.2.5:16.2 - Narrowing-source rule
Closure may rise because evidence eliminates rivals, governance temporarily binds a route, or protocol requires fixation under time pressure. State the source of narrowing because different sources imply different reopen expectations.

#### C.2.5:16.3 - Partial-closure rule
Closure may be local rather than global. A note can be closed enough for one route while remaining open about broader explanation or classification; a prompt may be fixed enough to hold one question steady while still open enough that rival answers remain live. Publish that locality explicitly.

### C.2.5:17 - Continuing and Withdrawn Authority Handling

#### C.2.5:17.1 - Authority retention rule
If higher `CD` carried endpoint expectations, guard claims, or route commitments, a closure drop must say which consequences remain and which are withdrawn. Treat any actual authority-relation change separately under its direct pattern, as required by `A.16.2`.

#### C.2.5:17.2 - Admissible retreat record
An admissible retreat through `reopen`, `sketchBackoff`, or `respecify` should retain:

- the prior closure state;
- the reason the prior fixation no longer holds;
- the assumption or route being relaxed;
- the still-binding remainder, if any.

This prevents false continuity after retreat.

#### C.2.5:17.3 - Closure versus obligation boundary
High `CD` may coexist with obligations. When prose treats "closed" as "must now be done", use `A.2.8` to identify the duty bearer, duty, and instituting rule and basis; retain the applicable `governingPatternRef` or `authoritySourceRef` for that obligation claim.

### C.2.5:18 - Review Matrix and Reopen Tests

#### C.2.5:18.1 - Review matrix
An assurance reader should ask:

- what was narrowed;
- what evidence, choice or applicable rule supports that narrowing, with a `governingPatternRef`, `authoritySourceRef` or guard when one is used;
- what would reopen it;
- which gate, release, work, evidence-use, assurance, policy, or adjudication claims depend on the stated closure conditions and remain supported;
- whether the publication distinguishes local closure from whole-case finality.

#### C.2.5:18.2 - False-finality test
When a receiving action relies on "final", "settled", or "decided", check the actual scope and source of fixation and any applicable guard. A final-sounding word alone does not establish those conditions.

#### C.2.5:18.3 - Cross-facet reminder
Low `CD` does not imply low articulation, low anchoring, or poor representation.

#### C.2.5:18.4 - Split-closure review case
A publication may be closed enough for immediate local work use or reliance use while remaining open about broader explanation, long-horizon consequences, or alternative classification. Allow the split when locality is explicit; reject prose that advertises whole-case finality when only one language-state segment is fixed.

### C.2.5:End

## C.2.6 - `U.LanguageStateAnchoringMode` — How Is the Episteme Anchored?

> **Type:** Definitional (D)
> **Status:** Stable
> **Normativity:** Normative unless marked informative

**Plain-name.** Language-state anchoring mode.

**Use this pattern when.** Use C.2.6 when how an episteme is anchored changes its interpretation, comparison or use. The mode can distinguish bodily enactment, traces, model state, document mediation, an operator loop or an explicit mixture. An ordinary description of the anchor is sufficient unless the receiving use needs a declared mode.

**What goes wrong if missed.** A prose note hides an embodied, trace-based, model-latent, or operator-loop cue; bridge-loss notes disappear; and the final publication face is mistaken for the original anchoring regime.

**What this buys.** A nominal Characteristic for comparing how epistemes are anchored, independently of their publication forms. Evidence and loss accounts can then address the actual anchoring relation.

### C.2.6:1 - Problem frame
Published position claims in the declared language-state chart over `U.CharacteristicSpace` differ not only by articulation and closure, but by how the `U.Episteme` named in that claim is anchored to bodies, traces, model states, documents, or operator loops.

### C.2.6:2 - Problem
When a comparison or use depends on anchoring, leaving it implicit can hide the difference between a bodily cue, a trace and a description of either. A representation label alone may leave that difference unresolved.

### C.2.6:3 - Forces
| Force | Tension |
|---|---|
| **Embodiment vs abstraction** | Preserve embodied and operator-facing cases while making their anchoring explicit. |
| **Small core vs real diversity** | Keep the core compact while allowing multiple admissible anchoring regimes. |
| **Comparability vs oversimplification** | Compare anchoring regimes while retaining distinctions that a text-vs-nontext split hides. |

### C.2.6:4 - Solution
`U.LanguageStateAnchoringMode` is a nominal characteristic that states the primary anchoring regime of the `U.Episteme` named by the current position claim: bodily enactment, trace, model state, document, operator loop, or an explicit mixed regime. When a receiving episteme has a different anchoring regime from its source, distinguish both. A change of publication form alone does not establish that difference.

#### C.2.6:4.0a - Kind and characteristic boundary

`U.LanguageStateAnchoringMode` is the Characteristic of an episteme assessed in the declared language-state chart. Its readings belong to a nominal Scale; the chart slot binds that Characteristic to its Scale under A.18/A.19. The mode identifies how the episteme is anchored. Any evidence, currentness or action claim still needs the relation and conditions that establish it.

#### C.2.6:4.1 - Starter family
| Mode | Reading | Possible witness of anchoring |
|---|---|---|
| `AM.EmbodiedFelt` | bodily or kinesthetic anchoring matters directly | embodiment note, felt trace, human witness |
| `AM.TraceAnchored` | traces or observations anchor the episteme | trace references, measured events, observations |
| `AM.ModelLatent` | latent or internal model state is the key anchor | model-state refs, probe results, latent summaries |
| `AM.DocumentMediated` | document or description is the principal anchor | documents, cards, method-description text |
| `AM.OperatorLoop` | the episteme is directly tied to operator intervention or console control | operator witness, console event, policy hook |
| `AM.Mixed` | more than one anchoring mode matters substantively | explicit component list and why the mix matters |

#### C.2.6:4.2 - Contribution boundary

The mode characterizes anchoring of the episteme named in the position claim. Representation factors describe how information is represented; closure describes fixity. Neither follows from an anchoring mode. Apply the rule for any further claim, such as an evidence relation or permission to act.

If embodiment matters, it shall be declared here or immediately beside this characteristic rather than being hidden inside representation talk.

#### C.2.6:4.3 - Mixed-mode rule
`AM.Mixed` is admissible only when the component modes are named explicitly. "Mixed" shall not stand in for an undetermined anchoring mode.

#### C.2.6:4.4 - Bridge implications
An anchoring shift can matter when a receiving use needs a semantic relation between local senses from different semantic contexts. A receiving episteme anchored in a document may depend on a source anchored in bodily experience or model state. That difference may affect the evidence or loss account for the semantic correspondence. Use F.9 to state and test the Bridge and the separate bounded-use claim, with its evidence and loss account. Use F.9.1 only for a separate optional stance note about that claim.

### C.2.6:5 - Archetypal Grounding
**Tell.** A felt cue, a controller-side probe score, and a textual design note may all be early cues, but they are anchored differently.

**Show (System).** An alert episteme directly tied to operator intervention or console control has mode `AM.OperatorLoop`, even when displayed as text.

**Show (Episteme).** An episteme published from a model-probe cue grounded in latent state has mode `AM.ModelLatent` even when rendered into prose.

### C.2.6:6 - Bias-Annotation
The pattern prompts authors to declare anchoring when wording such as "the system wants" or "the note suggests" leaves the anchor unclear.

### C.2.6:7 - Conformance Checklist
- `CC-C.2.6-1` Anchoring mode **SHALL NOT** be inferred from publication phrasing alone when it matters for source use, reliance, or bridge interpretation.
- `CC-C.2.6-2` Embodiment-sensitive or operator-loop cases **SHOULD** declare the embodiment or operator anchor explicitly.
- `CC-C.2.6-3` `U.LanguageStateAnchoringMode` **MUST NOT** be collapsed into `U.LanguageStateRepresentationFactorBundle`.
- `CC-C.2.6-4` Mixed-mode declarations **SHALL** list their component modes explicitly.

### C.2.6:8 - Common Anti-Patterns and How to Avoid Them
- **Text-only illusion.** Treating every cue as document-mediated because it has been written down.
- **Representation capture.** Using symbolic/distributed labels to hide world-anchoring distinctions.
- **Embodiment mystification.** Treating bodily or operator-loop cues as beyond explicit publication.
